title: Managed Device Baseline
subtitle: The standard every managed device meets, from purchase order to disposal.
purpose: A build and lifecycle standard, organised the way the work actually happens. The NIST device guide answers 'what does 800-53 require'; this answers 'what do I do to this laptop, and in what order'. Same underlying controls, technician's sequence instead of the auditor's.
note: Every item cites the 800-53 control it satisfies and, where the assessment can check it, the tool control that verifies it. Items marked Mandatory are the non-negotiable set — a device that misses one is not a managed device, it is an unmanaged device with an asset tag.

stages.Title: 1. Procurement and intake
stages.Description: Decisions made before the device is touched. Getting these wrong is expensive to undo — hardware that cannot meet the baseline has to be replaced, not reconfigured.

Items.Requirement: Hardware supports TPM 2.0, Secure Boot and UEFI
Items.Why: Without a TPM there is no hardware root of trust: BitLocker falls back to a password, Windows Hello cannot bind a credential to the device, and Device Health Attestation reports nothing at all.
Items.How: Confirm on the quote before purchase. Verify after unboxing with tpm.msc or Get-Tpm, and confirm Secure Boot is enabled in firmware.

Items.Requirement: Device is recorded in the asset register before it is issued
Items.Why: A device that was never recorded cannot be detected as missing. The gap between what was bought and what is enrolled is where devices quietly disappear.
Items.How: Record serial, model, purchase date, assigned user and expected refresh date. Reconcile against the Intune device list on a fixed cadence.

Items.Requirement: Device is registered for zero-touch provisioning where the vendor supports it
Items.Why: Autopilot / ADE enrolment cannot be skipped by the end user. Manual enrolment can, and the devices that skip it are invisible until something goes wrong on them.
Items.How: Windows Autopilot via the hardware hash or vendor registration; Apple Business Manager for macOS and iOS; Android zero-touch or Knox.

Items.Requirement: Firmware and BIOS administration is password-protected
Items.Why: An unprotected firmware menu lets anyone with five minutes of physical access disable Secure Boot, change the boot order, and boot the machine from a USB stick — around every control above the firmware.
Items.How: Set a BIOS/UEFI supervisor password as part of the build, managed centrally where the vendor supports it (Dell Command, HP Sure Admin, Lenovo Think BIOS).

stages.Title: 2. Provisioning and enrolment
stages.Description: Bringing the device under management. Nothing in later stages can be enforced until this is done, so this is where an incomplete build causes the most damage.

Items.Requirement: Device is enrolled in Intune and has an Entra device identity
Items.Why: Without a device identity there is nothing for Conditional Access to evaluate, no target for policy, and no way to distinguish this machine from an unknown one.
Items.How: Entra join (or hybrid join for domain-attached estates) plus automatic Intune enrolment. Confirm the device appears in both Entra and Intune before hand-over.

Items.Requirement: Enrolment restrictions block platforms that cannot meet this baseline
Items.Why: A baseline that a device is allowed to enrol without meeting is a suggestion. Restrictions are what make it a standard.
Items.How: Intune enrolment restrictions blocking personally-owned platforms and unsupported OS versions, with a documented exception path.

Items.Requirement: The local administrator password is unique per device and rotated automatically
Items.Why: A shared local admin password means one recovered credential unlocks every device that shares it. This is the single most common way a single-machine compromise becomes an estate-wide one.
Items.How: Windows LAPS deployed via Intune, escrowing per-device passwords to Entra ID with automatic rotation. Remove any pre-existing shared local account as part of the build.

Items.Requirement: The day-to-day user account is not a local administrator
Items.Why: Most endpoint malware needs administrative rights to persist. Removing standing admin from daily accounts removes that step entirely.
Items.How: Standard user by default, with an approved elevation path (Intune Endpoint Privilege Management or an equivalent) for the cases that genuinely need it.

Items.Requirement: Full-disk encryption is on, with the recovery key escrowed
Items.Why: This is what turns a stolen laptop into a hardware loss instead of a reportable data breach. An unescrowed key turns a forgotten PIN into permanent data loss.
Items.How: BitLocker with TPM + PIN, key escrowed to Entra ID (Windows). FileVault with key escrow via Intune (macOS). Confirm the key is visible in Entra before hand-over — an escrow that silently failed looks identical to one that worked.

Items.Requirement: Phishing-resistant or biometric sign-in is configured
Items.Why: Replaces the password on the device with a credential bound to that device's TPM, which cannot be phished, replayed, or reused anywhere else.
Items.How: Windows Hello for Business, or a FIDO2 security key where a shared or kiosk device makes Hello impractical.

stages.Title: 3. Hardening
stages.Description: The configuration baseline applied to every managed device. These are policy-enforced rather than build-time steps, so they also self-heal on devices that drift.

Items.Requirement: A security configuration baseline is assigned
Items.Why: Per-device configuration drifts. A defined baseline makes drift visible and reversible instead of invisible and permanent.
Items.How: Intune Security Baselines (Windows, Defender for Endpoint, Edge). Where local deviation is required, document the deviation and why.

Items.Requirement: Anti-malware and EDR are running, up to date, and tamper-protected
Items.Why: Signature scanning alone stops commodity malware. EDR telemetry is what lets anyone reconstruct what happened after a real intrusion.
Items.How: Defender antivirus with real-time protection, cloud-delivered protection and tamper protection on, plus Defender for Endpoint onboarding. Where a third-party EDR is the standard, evidence coverage from that console and record it as the compensating control.

Items.Requirement: Attack Surface Reduction rules are in Block mode
Items.Why: ASR blocks the specific techniques that start most endpoint intrusions — Office spawning processes, obfuscated script execution, credential theft from LSASS — without needing to detect the malware itself.
Items.How: Deploy the office-macro, script and credential-theft rule set in Block mode. Audit mode first for a fortnight if the estate has unknown line-of-business software, but Audit mode is not the destination.

Items.Requirement: The host firewall is enabled on all profiles
Items.Why: The host firewall is the control that still applies when the laptop is on a hotel or home network with no perimeter in front of it.
Items.How: Intune firewall policy enabling all profiles with inbound blocked by default, exceptions documented.

Items.Requirement: The screen locks automatically and requires re-authentication
Items.Why: Covers the unattended-desk case, which is the most common physical exposure in any office and the only one that happens daily.
Items.How: Maximum inactivity timeout with credential re-entry (15 minutes typical for workstations, 5 for mobile). Enforced by compliance policy, not left to the user.

Items.Requirement: Removable storage is blocked or restricted to approved encrypted media
Items.Why: USB is the exfiltration path that leaves no network trace and no audit log unless something is watching the endpoint itself.
Items.How: Defender device control allowing approved encrypted drives by hardware ID, or Endpoint DLP auditing and blocking copies of sensitive content to removable media.

Items.Requirement: Corporate data on mobile devices is containerised
Items.Why: Personally-owned phones will hold corporate mail whether or not anyone planned for it. Containerisation governs the data without managing the personal device.
Items.How: App Protection Policies (MAM) requiring a PIN, blocking save-as to personal storage, and enforcing selective wipe. Conditional launch to block jailbroken or rooted devices and those below a minimum patch level.

stages.Title: 4. In service
stages.Description: Ongoing obligations. A device that met the baseline on day one and has not been patched since is not a compliant device — it is a compliant photograph of a device.

Items.Requirement: Operating system updates install within a defined window
Items.Why: Nearly all exploited endpoint vulnerabilities have a patch available at the time of exploitation. The window between release and installation is the actual exposure.
Items.How: Update rings with a deferral period and an enforced deadline, plus a compliance policy setting a minimum OS version so an unpatched device loses access rather than quietly persisting.

Items.Requirement: Third-party applications are patched too
Items.Why: Browsers, PDF readers, Java and conferencing clients are the most exploited software on any endpoint, and Windows Update does not touch them.
Items.How: RMM-driven third-party patching, or Intune Enterprise App Management where the catalogue covers the estate. Whichever is used, someone must be able to answer 'what is unpatched right now'.

Items.Requirement: Non-compliant devices actually lose access
Items.Why: Compliance state that carries no consequence is a report, not a control. This is the item that gives every control above it teeth.
Items.How: Conditional Access requiring a compliant or Entra-joined device on the sessions that matter. Confirm the policy is enforced, not report-only — a report-only policy looks identical in the portal until you check the state.

Items.Requirement: Corporate data does not sync to unmanaged devices
Items.Why: An unrestricted sync client replicates an entire document library onto a personal machine that meets none of this baseline, and does it silently.
Items.How: Restrict OneDrive sync to domain-joined or Entra-joined devices by tenant GUID, and use Conditional Access session controls to make unmanaged browsers read-only.

Items.Requirement: Device inventory is reconciled on a fixed cadence
Items.Why: Devices that appear in one system and not another are the ones that go missing. Stale Intune records also hide genuinely absent hardware.
Items.How: Reconcile Intune against the RMM and the asset register quarterly. Investigate anything that has not checked in for 30 days rather than deleting it.

Items.Requirement: Loss or theft has a reporting path with a target time
Items.Why: Encryption protects a lost device only until someone guesses the PIN. The response window is what limits that exposure, and staff will not report quickly if they do not know how.
Items.How: A documented path staff actually know, a named person authorised to trigger the wipe, and a target reporting time. Test it once a year the way you would test a backup.

stages.Title: 5. Offboarding and disposal
stages.Description: The stage that is skipped most often, and the one that leaves data outside your control when it is. Everything here is off-tenant evidence: the assessment can see the account, never the hardware.

Items.Requirement: Device return is part of the leaver checklist, alongside account disablement
Items.Why: Account disablement is automated and device return is not, so the two drift apart. Stale licensed accounts in the tenant are the visible symptom; the unreturned laptop is the part nobody sees.
Items.How: One checklist covering account disablement, device return, badge return and key return, with completed instances retained. Reconcile returns against the asset register.

Items.Requirement: Returned devices are wiped before reissue
Items.Why: A device reissued without a wipe carries the previous user's cached credentials, tokens and local data to its next holder.
Items.How: Intune retire or wipe, then a fresh provisioning run through stage 2. Retire removes company data; wipe returns the device to factory state — pick deliberately, and record which was used.

Items.Requirement: Disposed devices are sanitised, with evidence retained
Items.Why: This is the most commonly missing piece of evidence in an MSP-managed environment, because disposal usually happens outside the managed-service scope and nobody owns it.
Items.How: Cryptographic erase on encrypted drives (destroy the key), or a certified disposal vendor issuing per-asset certificates of destruction. Retain certificates with the asset register. Note that a remote wipe is a request, not a guarantee, and does not substitute for sanitising recovered hardware.

Items.Requirement: The device record is closed out, not just deleted
Items.Why: Deleting the record destroys the evidence that the device was disposed of properly. An auditor asking what happened to serial X needs an answer.
Items.How: Mark the asset as disposed with the date, method and certificate reference. Remove the Entra and Intune objects only after that record exists.
